A) Toward the unity of their life in Christ...

25. Following in Mother Rosa's footsteps, the Daughters of Saint Anne, “seeking God solely and above everything else,” strive to unite contemplation with apostolic zeal449 and seek, like Christ, in the intimacy of prayer, the encounter with the Father in a relationship of intense and tender filial love450; and by entering into the paschal mystery they associate themselves with the work of redemption and the spreading of the Kingdom451.

26. Imitating Mary's permanent dialogue with the Lord, constantly present in her life, the Daughters of Saint Anne direct their prayer, discovering in it day by day the Father's message452, which they live with the enthusiasm of a poor heart that, knowing itself loved by the Lord, hopes for everything from him; and they advance joyfully on the way of charity453.

27. In this perspective the whole day of the Daughters of Saint Anne, with its many and varied activities, becomes an authentic and constant prayer454. Wholly devoted to the salvation of the world, “a divine work that transcends all human strength and human wisdom”455, they feel sustained and enlivened by moments of intense prayer in which, discovering God's saving plan, they find in Christ the unifying center that gives unity to their life woven of prayer and action.

The unifying center of their life,

28. Christ, remaining precisely the principle and source of the unity of their life, draws all the activity of the Daughters of Saint Anne toward himself and makes them effective apostles of the Gospel, giving them a sensitivity that enables them to understand the needs of their contemporaries and to become incarnate in the historical reality of the moment.

they discover the divine will.

29. Naturally, achieving unity of life requires knowing, accepting and fulfilling the Father's will456, and this knowledge, understanding and carrying out of God's concrete will “hic et nunc” is a divine mystery accessible to human beings only through “prayer and the spirit of prayer”457, which, as two aspects of a single reality, interpenetrate and condition each other.

With the light and strength gained in prayer and kept through the spirit of prayer, one will be able to recognize and do God's will during the day and so achieve, ever more deeply, inner unity and, with it, maturity and perfection.

Hence the fundamental importance, for people in general and for women religious in particular, of acquiring the spirit of prayer and prayer itself as an indispensable means of achieving this unity. Prayer, in turn, is nourished above all by participation in the Liturgy and by the intimacy of personal conversation with God.

Through liturgical participation

30. The life received in Baptism keeps growing, and it develops and is strengthened especially through the Liturgy, considered as the exercise of Christ's priestly office, which he uses to sanctify humanity and in which he himself mystically offers to God full public worship459.

31. In carrying out “the threefold priestly, prophetic and royal office God has entrusted to them”460, believers who take part in the Liturgy through the Sacraments become the true worshipers the Father seeks461 and proclaim the Lord's death until he comes462, foretasting the reality they will share in the holy City of Jerusalem, toward which they journey as pilgrims463.

... and personal prayer

32. Yet it is personal prayer that precedes, accompanies, continues and develops authentic liturgy, since “the spiritual life is not limited solely to participation in the liturgy”464. Personal prayer is in fact the preparation for and prolongation of liturgical life, so that there is no conflict between these two ways of praying; each necessarily calls for the other, and both, like two converging lines tending toward God, meet and complement each other in a wonderful harmony springing from their shared inner nature, namely that they are simply two different ways of expressing communion of life with Christ.

33. Faithful, then, to the exhortations of Jesus and his Disciples to pray “without ceasing”465, and following the example of the first Christians, who “devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers”466, the Daughters of Saint Anne pray unceasingly to the Father in the secret of their hearts and, called together by the Word, gather in fraternal communion to pray together458; and, in a constant longing for conversion that directs them toward the Eucharist, the highest expression of community union, they join in the praise of the universal Church according to the spirit of the liturgical seasons.

B) Called together by the word...

34. “The word of God is living and active”467, “which is able to build you up and give you the inheritance among all who are sanctified”468; and it is by the power of this Word that the Daughters of Saint Anne, at Jesus' invitation, “come, follow me”469, having left everything470 and regarding everything “as loss because of the surpassing value of knowing Christ Jesus (my) Lord”471, commit themselves to a life bearing witness to God's presence and redeeming love for humanity.

Personal meditation

35. In carrying out this ecclesial mission, the Daughters of Saint Anne, while working out their own sanctification, are also a means of sanctification for others472; and so they need unceasing prayer473 that is a genuine expression of their consecration and a source of apostolic fruitfulness; indeed, only in the intimacy of a living and permanent encounter with Christ, in filial relationship with the Father and through the power of the Spirit, can they find the one reason for their life.

The reality of life, a divine message,

36. Therefore the Daughters of Saint Anne, like Mother Rosa before them, must be “women of prayer” who, docilely open to the Word, discover in it God as a Person; in his infinite love he makes himself present in their lives to establish a permanent dialogue with them.

37. Interiorizing the Word is impossible without a religious silence that allows one to listen to God474, who reveals himself as “the gentle whisper of a light breeze”475; and only the humble can enjoy his intimacy476, since they alone can recognize the greatness of divine revelation: “Has anything so great as this ever happened or has its like ever been heard of? So acknowledge today and take to heart”477.

38. Divine revelation, however, culminates in Jesus Christ478, the true “sacrament of encounter with God”; in him, the Word made flesh, the Father addresses humanity479, and in turn human beings, moved by the Holy Spirit, give their answer to the Father “through Christ our Lord.” A filial answer that expresses the ineffable mystery of being children in the Son, “by whom we cry, Abba! Father!”480.

39. Prayer, then, a filial dialogue with the Father in Christ, makes transparent the divine plan in history481, which embodies in every person and thing a message of his love.

Awareness of this truth makes prayer a truly vital activity, in which one perceives and understands ever better God's presence and action in the personal, community and world events of each day. The reality of life, become the matter of personal prayer, prompts a demanding response.

40. The Daughters of Saint Anne, immersed in a secularized world, feel ever more deeply the responsibility of sharing “the joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of the people of this age, especially those who are poor or in any way afflicted”482; they become convinced that prayer cannot be confined to isolated moments of their day but is a constant need that must grow in depth and intensity as their apostolic commitment immerses them ever further in the life of the world483.

41. Prayer, moreover, is one of the perfect gifts “coming down from above, from the Father of lights”484, since it actualizes the real, though still hidden, relationship between God and his creature. Human response in our present condition is not always easy485, so that prayer is a demanding exercise that often becomes a real sacrifice; but it would be illusory to put it off to the whim of a free moment or a moment of fervor on the pretext of a need for authenticity.

42. Prayer therefore requires an asceticism that develops and strengthens throughout the day an inner attitude of silence, recollection and self-mastery, so as to achieve the most favorable conditions for the one praying: physically alert, not exhausted by excessive fatigue, psychologically serene, free from worldly images, spiritually recollected and supernaturally open to receive God and his message486. To this end it is essential to create in the Community a supernatural atmosphere that fosters prayer and, centering affectivity on God, gives fullness and joy to its life487.

Community meditation

43. Inspired by the example of the “poor of Yahweh,” who gathered in the Synagogue to hear the Word of God488; by the example of Jesus, who took part in these gatherings489; and by the example of Mary, persevering in prayer with the Apostles while awaiting the Spirit the Comforter490, the Daughters of Saint Anne seek in the shared, meditative study of God's Word a living encounter with the Lord who has called them together, and through a mutual and lively sharing of their reflections they grow in the knowledge of God in Jesus Christ and in love for one another.

44. In this biblical reflection, searching together will help to discover better the Message the Lord addresses to the Community through his Words and through past history and daily events. In this spiritual dialogue, with everyone's contribution, the meaning the Word takes on in the Community's concrete situation is deepened, and each is enlightened, enriched and moved to live her response of faith with greater ardor.

45. Moreover, sharing one's thoughts awakens and deepens friendship, because, called together by Love and committed to seeking the same Good491, the Daughters of Saint Anne realize that each of them can discover a different aspect of the Truth, which is inexhaustible in itself; and in this mutual deepening of the Divine Word they exercise the prophetic function of the Community.

Celebration of the Word

Listening, song and prayer in response

46. The celebration of the Word, the expression of a Community that listens, reflects and “responds in song and prayer”492 so as then to carry out the divine message in life, is the logical consequence of the sincerity with which the Community commits itself to imitating Christ and devotes itself to the salvation of the People of God.

in the presence of the Lord.

47. The Assembly engaged in celebrating the Word particularly enjoys the Lord's presence493; and, gaining a deeper knowledge of the Mystery of Salvation, it is vitally directed toward the sacraments, above all the Eucharist. Hence the importance of promoting these celebrations, especially in preparation for the most solemn feasts of the Liturgical Year and of the religious Family, as well as on community anniversaries and on some weekdays of Advent and Lent494.

Spiritual reading, monthly retreat, annual retreat

48. In the dynamic of listening to the Word, spiritual reading, the monthly retreat and the [annual] retreat are particularly important as effective supports.

Spiritual reading, which pursues an aim that is not scholarly or purely intellectual but sapiential, is a precious help in being formed in faith and living one's friendship with God more fully495. Obviously the book par excellence is and always will be Sacred Scripture: “Religious should have the sacred Scriptures in hand every day, so that by reading and meditating on the holy books they may learn the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ”496.

Moreover, the monthly retreat and the days devoted to the Spiritual Exercises, by fostering more intensely the restoration of the energies of the spirit, foster the interiorization of the paschal mystery, while enlivening the commitment to respond to one's vocation in fidelity to one's charism.

C)... They cultivate the sense of penance...

49. Through Baptism believers are “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people saved”497, but the existential reality of each day shows humanity's sinful condition498 and therefore its need for constant conversion and penance: “repent, and believe in the good news”499, because “only by putting to death what is old can one attain renewal of life”500.

50. The Church, holy and blameless yet at the same time fallible in her members, “never neglects penance”501, urging the faithful “always to carry in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our mortal flesh”502, so as thus to share in Christ's work and expiation. Moreover, the Church emphasizes that the precept of penance must be fulfilled more perfectly by those who, called to follow more closely the Lord's “self-emptying,” profess the Evangelical Counsels503.

In union with Christ Crucified

51. Convinced of the perennial need for a penitential attitude, the Daughters of Saint Anne also find in their spirituality a pressing reason that urges them to practice penance in humble acknowledgment of their poverty, which stands out still more in the light of God's holiness (cf. Is 6:5) and shines in their hearts as the fruit of intimate union with Christ in the mystery of his utmost poverty: the cross504.

52. Indeed Christ, the Servant of Yahweh, “who has borne our infirmities and carried our diseases”505, confirms by a life of penance his unavoidable invitation: “If any want to become my followers, let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me”506. An invitation whose acceptance involves the whole person, since inner conversion gives rise to the need for a voluntary practice of mortification “beyond the renunciations imposed by the burden of daily life”507.

53. This is how Mother Rosa understood it, and to a heroic degree: as a seeker of God she lived not only the anguish of discovering herself to be a limited creature subject to sin, but also, like Christ, felt responsible for her guilty brothers and sisters508; her spirit of penance and her longing for bodily mortifications therefore have one source and one goal: Love509.

In the Sacrament of Penance

making the most of every daily circumstance

54. Her desire to be identified with her “Crucified Beloved” moves Mother Rosa always and everywhere to carry in her body the sufferings and death of Jesus, so that the life of Christ, made visible in her510, may become compassion for human frailty, redemption for others and a good for the Church511. Moreover, her love for the mystery of the cross becomes in her a living and concrete reality, so that she knows how to make every daily circumstance a means of redemption and a sure path to glorification512. The light of the resurrection thus illuminates the life of Mother Rosa, which, like Saint Paul's, was a constant preaching of Jesus Christ, and Jesus Christ crucified513.

they joyfully accept a life of renunciation.

55. Following in the Mother Foundress's footsteps, the Daughters of Saint Anne must therefore awaken in themselves the penitential sense that leads them to share in the self-emptying of the poor Christ who offers himself to the Father's saving will. In this context they must not only accept with joy the toils and pains of each day but also seek a poor manner of life, striving to acquire the “spirit of self-denial,” “so as to become accustomed to living in conformity with Christ Crucified and to renouncing promptly even things lawful in themselves but not fitting”514 for their consecration, convinced that they can never free themselves from the selfishness of a self-enclosed life without mortification, set, however, within the paschal joy of Christ's resurrection515.

In the Sacrament of Penance

56. It is not enough, however, to feel the call to conversion and respond to it; one must also approach the sacraments, through which the saving action flowing from Christ's death and resurrection is spread.

Christ, Lord and source of the sacraments and at the same time Sacrament of the Father's mercy, “who came to free man and give him strength”516, left the Church the sacrament of penance as a “sign” of a new encounter with him and with others; in this sacrament the sinner “obtains pardon from the mercy of God for the offense committed against him and is at the same time reconciled with the Church, which he has wounded by his sin”517.

57. The sacramental experience of God's forgiveness opens the members of the ecclesial Community to one another and makes possible the acknowledgment of failure and the healing of divisions through mutual forgiveness, because the whole Church, which feels involved in the sin of individuals, is also united with them at the moment of their conversion, sharing in the joy of reconciliation with a view to a new life: “This is the covenant that I will make after those days, says the Lord: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts”518.

58. In frequent confession, prepared for by the daily examination of conscience519 and made as a purification in the blood of Christ520, the Daughters of Saint Anne learn to submit their sins to the Church with a contrite heart so as “to be converted ever more to the Lord”521, in a religious act whose goal is the intensification of love for God and neighbor. In this way they benefit from the grace of the sacrament not only personally but also in restoring community union, both within the religious Family and within the great ecclesial family522.

In penitential celebrations

59. The penitential spirit is also fostered through community penitential celebrations, in which shared reflection on the Word of God leads to humble acknowledgment of sin, so that each ceases to regard herself as the center, measure and end of her thoughts and actions and begins to direct everything to God's glory and to union with others in the spirit of Christ's love. “Collective awareness of sin” is an eloquent witness to the communal character of conversion and an excellent preparation for receiving the grace of forgiveness in the Sacrament of Penance.

and on the threshold of Eternity

60. In the Church's penitential spirit, through the Sacrament of the Anointing of the sick, the sick are commended to the suffering and glorified Lord, that he may raise them up and save them523, and are exhorted to unite themselves freely to Christ's passion and death524, contributing by their sufferings to the good of the People of God525. The Anointing of the sick thus becomes a foretaste of joy in awaiting the Savior, since Christ, our life526, “will transform the body of our humiliation that it may be conformed to the body of his glory, by the power that also enables him to make all things subject to himself”527.

the Daughter of Saint Anne joyfully awaits the Lord's coming.

61. The Daughter of Saint Anne, aware that she bears within her the new creation, in an attitude of watchful expectation proper to her spirituality and motherly self-giving, approaches the final goal of her life encouraged by the words of Scripture she has often pondered in her heart: “I am coming soon; my reward is with me, to repay according to everyone's work”528; and in the joy and simplicity of a life offered to God as a holocaust529, she receives the holy Anointing, abandoning herself to the divine Will.

D)... Oriented toward the Eucharist, the highest expression of community...

62. The People of God finds the “visible and invisible” expression of its human-divine reality especially in the Eucharistic Liturgy, through which “the work of our redemption is accomplished”530. Indeed priests, “by Baptism bring people into the People of God; by the sacrament of Penance reconcile sinners with God and the Church; by the Oil of the sick relieve the sick; and especially by the celebration of Mass offer sacramentally the Sacrifice of Christ”531. That is why every sacrament depends on and derives from the Eucharist, which is “as it were the consummation of the spiritual life and the goal of all the sacraments”532.

The Lord's Supper

63. An indispensable element, root and hinge of every Christian community, is the celebration of the holy Eucharist533, since “in the full and active participation in the same Eucharist, in a single prayer, at one altar”534, the Community is integrated into the fullness of liturgical life; it offers the divine victim to God and itself along with it535; and, “then strengthened in Holy Communion by the Body of Christ, it shows in a concrete way its unity”536 in the bond of charity.

64. Each time the Eucharist is celebrated, the paschal Mystery of Christ is accomplished and made present, Christ “who by dying destroyed our death and by rising restored our life”537. Paschal redemption is thus perpetuated on the altar through a sensible and perceptible rite that changes the bread and wine, “fruit of the earth and of our work,” into the glorious Body and Blood of Christ538.

65. Moreover, Holy Mass or the Lord's Supper, which contains “the whole spiritual good of the Church and is the source and summit of all evangelization”539, unites in a single act of worship the liturgy of the word and the Eucharistic mystery, since the Lord's saving work, announced in the proclamation of the Word, is accomplished “in the very offering by which Christ ratified the new Covenant in his Blood”540.

66. The Eucharistic assembly is also the guarantee of the definitive encounter: a pledge of hope, food for the journey, a foretaste of the heavenly banquet541: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb”542. Thus the nourishment of Christ's Body and Blood makes the faithful sharers in his glorious life543: “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood have eternal life, and I will raise them up on the last day”544.

67. The Daughters of Saint Anne, called to live and bear witness in the Church, as a community and permanently, to the mystery of the Communion of Saints, find in the Eucharist the full expression of what their family must be: a unity of persons called together by the Father in the Body of the risen Christ545, for the glory of God and the life of the world.

68. Nourished, then, by the divine Word at the twofold table of Sacred Scripture and the Eucharist546, the Community, “as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God”547, prolongs union with Christ throughout the day548, contemplating in faith the gift received549. United in mutual love, it is renewed and grows joyfully in communion with the Father and with others, proclaiming in a life of poverty and motherly self-giving the coming of the glorious Christ.

Eucharistic adoration

69. Drawn into this Eucharistic dynamic, the Daughters of Saint Anne, faithful to their spirituality, which is eminently directed toward the Eucharist550, besides active participation in the Lord's Supper, show their attachment to the Word made flesh who came to dwell among us551 by remaining in his presence: “The spirit of my Institute is that in all Houses where there are sufficient means and members, perpetual adoration be held... or adoration for a whole day”552.

70. Adoration of Jesus in the Most Holy Eucharist must be understood in relation to the Mass and the mystery of salvation, since the divine “presence derives from the sacrifice and is directed toward both sacramental and spiritual communion”553; and so Eucharistic adoration “wonderfully nourishes the worship due to Christ in spirit and truth”554.

Visits to the Blessed Sacrament

71. The Daughters of Saint Anne, who have fidelity to their vocation at heart, commit themselves to “daily dialogue with Christ, visiting him in the tabernacle and practicing personal worship of the Holy Eucharist”555. Responding thus to the Lord's permanent presence in the sacred Species, they enjoy his intimate friendship, pray for the salvation of the world and nourish the right dispositions for celebrating the Lord's memorial each day by virtue of their royal priesthood556.

E)... They join in the universal praise of the Church...

Divine Office

72. After the Eucharistic celebration, it is principally through the Divine Office that the Church “praises the Lord without ceasing and intercedes for the salvation of the whole world”557, sanctifying the hours of the day558 in union with the prayer of praise that Jesus Christ raises to the Father as High Priest of humanity559.

73. By reciting the Divine Office, the Daughters of Saint Anne join in the eternal praise of the Word and “share in the greatest honor of Christ's Bride, for by offering these praises to God they are standing before God's throne in the name of the Church their Mother”560, and they commit themselves to a life that glorifies God.

74. Moreover, the Divine Office, a whole made up of psalms, hymns and scriptural readings expressing the hope of salvation that finds its living center in Christ and his Passover, represents for the Community of the Daughters of Saint Anne the prayerful expression of what it intends to be and achieve in its life561.

75. The recitation of the Divine Office thus becomes a prolongation of the Eucharistic celebration and spreads its sanctifying power through the various hours of the day, enabling us to live fully the mystery of Christ's Passover. This mystery becomes more evident in the course of the liturgical year, in which the Church progressively relives “the Work of Salvation of her divine Spouse”562.

F)... According to the spirit of the liturgical seasons...

The liturgical year

76. The liturgical year, a living and effective commemoration of the mystery of Salvation, presents Christ himself, who, ever living in his Church, “continues the journey of immense mercy that he lovingly began in this mortal life”563. It is not, then, a mere historical commemoration of the various events of Jesus' life, but rather the perennial and effective presence, in the liturgical Year, of the mystery of Christ, who works and acts as a great sign of salvation.

77. The mystical reality present in every stage of the liturgical year is particularly meaningful for the Daughters of Saint Anne564, whose charism is centered on the History of salvation; therefore the Community, consistent with its spirituality, lives with special intensity the season of Advent, which recalls the waiting for the Messiah, and that of Lent, which in its twofold baptismal and penitential aspect brings out more vividly the mystery of the poverty of Christ, the “servant of Yahweh,” as it prepares for the joy of the resurrection.

78. Renewed thus in their spirituality of expectation and gift, the Daughters of Saint Anne, active witnesses of the Resurrection and a sign of waiting for the coming of the Lord Jesus, sustained by the strength of God's grace, with the help of the Holy Spirit and in communion with the destiny of the sacrificed Lamb, journey toward the future and lasting city565, making use of each day's events to deserve to arrive “through the cross... at the light that knows no setting”566.

And on this journey toward the Homeland, feeling united with the heavenly Church, they venerate above all the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God; they honor with special devotion her holy Parents, Joachim and Anne, and remain faithful to the particular devotion the Institute has always shown to Saint Joseph, Saint Francis of Assisi and Saint Michael the Archangel. Nor do they forget their loved ones who have already left this earth, for whom they constantly offer suffrages.

Devotion to Most Holy Mary

79. Indissolubly joined to her Son's work of Salvation567, Mary is venerated by the Church with special love throughout the liturgical year, since, present in Christ's life and sacrifice568, she continues to be present in its re-enactment.

80. “All generations will call me blessed”569, Mary said in her canticle; and this praise, which humanity continues to repeat to her without ceasing, has become the expression of universal love for her who, “redeemed in a more sublime manner by reason of the merits of her Son”570, shared as intimately as a human creature can in Christ's intentions, actions and glory. Her humble response of faith to the Father's merciful Plan has made her the most sublime model to study and imitate; and so Mary's life has become a perennial liturgy, and her person is constantly present to God and to humanity as the history of salvation unfolds571.

Mother of the Church and model of virtue,

embodied ideal of the Daughter of Saint Anne,

81. Placed within the Mystical Body, Mary is also Mother of the Church, which contemplates in her “with joy, as in a most pure image, what she herself wholly desires and hopes to be”572; therefore believers raise their eyes to the Blessed Virgin, “who shines forth as the model of virtues for the whole community of the elect”573.

82. The Daughters of Saint Anne, committed by their virginal consecration in the Family of the holy Mother of Mary to a life of deep intimacy with the Lord in apostolic service, see in Mary also the living and concrete realization of their ideal, and therefore, consistent with their spirituality and origins, they make their own the words of the Liturgy: “Draw us, O Immaculate Virgin; we will run after you in the fragrance of your perfumes”574.

a “sign” of hope and consolation.

83. To this end they contemplate her united with Jesus in the mystery of his redeeming poverty; through her life they discover the figure and message of Anne, her holy Mother, and, celebrating her mysteries in the light of the history of salvation, with ardent zeal and devout hearts they implore the help of her intercession for the whole pilgrim people, “as a sign of sure hope and solace until the day of the Lord shall come”575.

In communion with the heavenly Church

United with all who belong to Christ,

84. The Liturgy, which shows the genuine nature of the Church as a community of faith, hope and charity, also highlights in the course of the liturgical year the union among those who belong to Christ, whether they are still pilgrims on earth, or, having fallen asleep in the Lord's peace, enjoy glory “beholding clearly God himself, triune and one, as he is”576, or are still being purified.

they proclaim the wonders he has worked in his Servants,

85. By virtue of this solidarity in Christ, the liturgy, which gathers the whole People of God chiefly around the altar, proclaims in celebrating the Feasts of the Saints “the wonderful works of Christ in his servants and offers the faithful fitting examples for their imitation”577, imploring God's blessings through their merits578.

intensifying their worship of God.

86. Thus the liturgy in honor of the Saints further enriches “the latreutic worship given to God the Father through Christ in the Spirit”579; it becomes an encouragement on the way to the Homeland and also kindles the hope of the definitive encounter with Christ, to celebrate in the joy of the eternal liturgy the marriage of the Lamb and the Church his Bride580.

87. Among the Saints who, “received into their heavenly home and present to the Lord, through him, with him and in him, do not cease to intercede with the Father for us”581, the Family of the Daughters of Saint Anne venerates above all the holy Mother of Mary582, whose presence determines the particular character of the Institute. Moreover, faithful to its origins, it embraces as its own the devotion Mother Rosa handed on to her daughters: to Saint Joachim, to Saint Joseph583, to Saint Francis of Assisi584 and to Saint Michael the Archangel585.

88. Devotion to Saint Anne, in its true nature, reminds the ecclesial community of a vivid manifestation of the presence and Face of God586. Indeed, the holy Mother of Mary, belonging to the stock of Jesse, is a hope and a fulfillment of the promise, because in giving life to Mary, “the plant from which the fruit of the world's salvation would be gathered”587, she cooperated in the imminent coming of the Lord.

89. In this perspective, set within the history of salvation, the figure of Saint Anne takes on new prominence; her message, bound up with her role as mother of Mary Immaculate588, proclaims the humble greatness of the “poor of Yahweh” who, pondering the “wonders” God worked for his people, confidently await the fulfillment of the prophecies: “A shoot shall come out from the stump of Jesse, and a branch shall grow out of his roots. The spirit of the Lord shall rest on him”589.

90. Mother Rosa understood that in Saint Anne it is God himself who speaks and shows the sign of his Kingdom590; and so, grasping the import of this message, she chose as the coat of arms of her Institute the symbol and words of the Prophet Isaiah: “Rod of Jesse”; and she gave devotion to the holy Mother a content of active love591, by virtue of which her daughters prolong the presence and mission of Saint Anne in the history of Salvation, which is still moving toward the Parousia.

91. Introductory Exposition

The religious vocation and the young woman in today's world

I. The fundamental idea of vocation

Vocation as dialogue

Vocation, a commitment to holiness.

1. Vocation, in the true sense of the word, means a call and requires a conscious and free response: this is dialogue, the basic element inseparable from the concept of vocation.

In the dialogue of vocation the initiative is God's, who reveals himself through a free gift and communicates himself to the human person to establish a covenant888. Vocation is not exhausted in an act that can be placed at a single precise moment; it is a continual invitation that unfolds until the parousia. The same is true of the response to vocation: God never interrupts the dialogue of vocation, “for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable”889; it is the human person who can interrupt this dialogue, temporarily or definitively.

2. Every person, in becoming aware of God's gift and responding positively to him, takes on a mission toward all people and in turn shares in the gift that others have received.

Vertical dialogue thus acquires a horizontal dimension, giving meaning “to the universal solidarity that binds people together”890. In this way, through communion with God and with others, by fidelity to commitment, the person attains holiness: “In the various kinds of life and the various tasks, one holiness is cultivated by all who are moved by the Spirit of God and, obeying the voice of the Father and worshiping God the Father in spirit and truth, follow the poor Christ”891.

In the “Following of Christ”

Vocation therefore leads the person to be fulfilled in his or her true human and Christian dimension: “As he who called you is holy, be holy yourselves in all your conduct; for it is written: “You shall be holy, for I am holy”892.

From this we conclude that every person and every Christian has one fundamental and irreversible vocation, realized in the state of life and the particular mission for which God has chosen him or her.

Eschatological witness.

The gift of one's whole life.

An ecclesial reality.

II. Religious vocation

3. What characterizes the religious vocation is “the gift of one's whole life to the service of God, thus living charity”893, through “a special consecration deeply rooted in baptismal consecration and a fuller expression of it”894.

The Council, by calling the evangelical counsels “a divine gift which the Church received from her Lord”895, places them within a reality of charismatic ministry, so that their institutionalization in religious life, “though not belonging to the hierarchical structure of the Church, nevertheless belongs to her life and holiness”896.

4. The Religious Vocation, a special charism of the Holy Spirit, is therefore first of all an ecclesial reality realized through the public profession of vows or similar commitments by which the faithful “bind themselves to the observance of the evangelical counsels”897, “following Christ who, virginal and poor, redeemed and sanctified all people by his obedience even unto death on the cross”898.

5. This implies following Christ as the Apostles did, who at his invitation “left everything and followed him”899; in the same way some Christians, by an outstanding gift of grace, are called to the life of chastity, poverty and obedience and also renounce positive human values “in order to live solely and as intensely as possible the fundamental mystery of the human person: a life of dialogue and communion with God and with others”900.

6. Although observance of the Counsels is a commitment the person takes on freely, giving himself “totally to God, loved above all”901, the initiative is really God's, who consecrates him through the Church; and by virtue of this consecration the religious will carry out in the Church a proper function of witness to eschatological values902.

“His witness, not abstract but existential, will be a sign of the transcendent holiness of the Church”903, showing to be possible, and making visible and verifiable to the whole People of God, the way of life “which Christ the Lord chose for himself and which the Virgin his Mother embraced”904, and at the same time showing the presence of the Kingdom of God among people.

Hence the religious vocation is a reality that the Church takes up, recognizes, ratifies and promotes, helping each person to discover his or her vocation within the historical context of each human life and guiding progressive choices.

Vocation and ministry.

At the service of the Church.

7. In the post-conciliar vision, vocation and ministry are correlative realities, because “the fundamental vocation to holiness is realized in the ministry to which God has called each person”905. The religious state, a particular way of living baptismal consecration, is also by its nature a call to the service of others. The religious, specially united to the Church and her mystery, has, like her, the task of bringing the Kingdom to maturity here on earth; and this is essentially apostolic.

8. “Let religious see well to it that the Church truly show forth Christ through them with ever increasing clarity to believers and unbelievers alike: Christ in contemplation on the mountain, or proclaiming the Kingdom of God to the multitudes, or healing the sick and maimed and turning sinners to a better life, or blessing children and doing good to all, always in obedience to the will of the Father who sent him”906.

Clearly religious consecration not only does not make “the religious a stranger to all other people, still less useless to the earthly city”907, but actually strengthens his capacity for effective service and total self-giving.

On the one hand, the religious must enter into the real world, today with greater boldness than in other ages; he cannot consider himself a stranger to human problems. On the other, in a world frighteningly tempted to let itself be submerged by temporal things, the religious must bear splendid and striking witness “that the world cannot be transfigured and offered to God without the spirit of the beatitudes”908.

III. As a Daughter of Saint Anne

In the Church: a diversity of religious families.

9. The religious vocation is specified according to the proper character of each Institute, “so that, by divine plan, a wonderful variety of religious communities grows up in the Church”909, “both for the advantage of their members and for the good of the whole Body of Christ”910.

The Holy Spirit gives a special charism to each Founder, and the Church, docilely following the divine inspiration, receives the rules they propose and authentically approves them, thus giving rise to the new religious family and at the same time committing herself, with her vigilant and protective authority, to fostering its growth according to the Founder's spirit911.

Rosa Gattorno: her first ideal.

10. In 1866912 Rosa Gattorno, moved by the Holy Spirit, founded by express command of Pius IX a new Institute, in which the Sisters “are to work for the growth of the holy faith and the care of the sick in their homes, and will also take in girls at risk, to whom they will teach Christian doctrine and needlework”913.

Rosa, believing at first that she saw in Mary Immaculate and Saint Francis of Assisi the models embodying her first inspiration, entrusted the Institute to their protection914; later, however, always faithfully listening to the divine will, she discovered in the figure of the holy Mother of Mary, who burst suddenly into her life, a sign of the Father's provident love915. Docile to the action of the Spirit, she once again sought confirmation of the divine plan in the Pope's word and, reassured by papal authorization, gave the Institute a new title: “Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate”916.

Saint Anne: the charism takes concrete form.

The Daughters of Saint Anne today.

Our time.

11. From then on, Saint Anne would be the figure who gives the Institute's life its decisive character917. Indeed, Saint Anne's presence gives the charism, already active in the first inspiration, a well-defined purpose and a spirituality of its own: “to present Christ to believers and unbelievers, collaborating in his saving work and showing them, in an attitude of poverty and motherly self-giving, the presence and mission of Saint Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate”918.

A purpose and spirituality that Mother Rosa lived with admirable simplicity of spirit, to the point of identifying herself with the mystery of Christ's poverty in its highest expression, the Crucified, while giving herself without reserve and without ever being exhausted, in a motherly presence that enlivened and made fruitful the “Work of God”919.

12. For the Daughters of Saint Anne, then, this fidelity and docility of Mother Rosa to the progressive development of the charism will be the reason for their existence in the Church and the motive of their own particular mission in spreading the Kingdom.

In this context, to be a Daughter of Saint Anne means to live religious consecration in the Family of the holy Mother, in that particular communion of life that springs from the commitment to reproduce, within the pilgrim Church, the spirit that informed the life of Our Lady's family920.

This implies for every Daughter of Saint Anne:

- docile and faithful listening to the action of the Holy Spirit, leading her to discover in the intimacy of prayer the Father's voice, which speaks in every event and through the “signs of the times”;

- an attitude of humble openness to God, aware that, called to be the “servant of the Lord,” she must seek only his good pleasure;

- an attitude of adoring gratitude to the Merciful God, who works wonders for his servant and makes her a witness and sign of his love for humanity;

- serene acceptance of redemptive suffering as the highest expression of her identification with the poor and crucified Christ;

- living always in the joyful certainty that the Risen Christ is, already in this world, her Friend, her Companion, her “Beloved”;

- an attitude of communion and solidarity with all her brothers and sisters called to salvation in Christ, on the basis of a life of real and effective poverty in a Church of the poor.

And all this permeated with that motherly tenderness which undoubtedly characterized Saint Anne's attitude toward her Immaculate Daughter and which Mother Rosa embodied and so strongly instilled in her daughters.

IV. The young woman and her concrete situation

13. “Institutes should provide their members with a suitable understanding both of the conditions of the times and of people and of the needs of the Church, so that, judging current circumstances wisely in the light of faith... they may be able to help others more effectively”921.

This passage leads us to consider, if only briefly, the situation of today's world and in particular of society as a whole: family, school and church.

Profound and rapid change.

The vital cell of society.

Contrasting situations.

The situation in the world922

14. “Today the human race is involved in a new stage of history, characterized by profound and rapid changes spreading by degrees around the whole world”923.

The most general aspects of these changes might be stated as follows:

- a true and profound social, cultural and religious transformation;

- growing awareness of the dignity and rights of the human person and consequently the demand for the integral advancement of women and of those living on the margins of society;

- the search for peace and solidarity among peoples, expressed especially in the struggle against racial discrimination;

- human insecurity, as a consequence of the contrast between progress in general and the poverty in which a large part of humanity languishes.

The situation of society

15. Every sector of social life presents today more than ever “contrasting aspects and situations; contrasts that involve the whole human person, who, precisely because essentially social, is often turned away from good and pushed toward evil in realizing his vocation by the very social context in which people are immersed from childhood, because of the tension arising from economic, political and social structures as well as from the pride and selfishness that corrupt the environment924.

Perhaps the most significant sign of today's society is the dynamism governing the process of socialization, which, though it brings “many advantages for strengthening and increasing the qualities of the human person,” is not without dangers925.

Bearing in mind that “young people exert very important influence in modern society”926, let us look at the most important aspects that can influence youth on the part of the family, the school and the church.

a) The Family. “Among the social ties necessary for man's development... the family, the primary and vital cell of society, corresponds most immediately to his innermost nature”927. In it “the various generations come together and help one another grow wiser and harmonize personal rights with the other requirements of social life”928. For this task to be fruitfully carried out, the family must have “an atmosphere animated by love and devotion to God and others, which favors the integral education of the children in a personal and social way”929.

This ideal vision of the family is unfortunately subject today to the pressure:

- of social tensions, especially demographic ones, which create many serious problems such as that of birth control;

- of the claim to the dignity and rights of women, which gives rise to a new kind of relationship between man and woman and which has had no small effect on the serious situations of family breakdown, a phenomenon more alarming today than ever;

- of the new shape and organization of family life, which, subject to an exaggerated assertion of personality and freedom, has provoked a conflict of generations with the consequent breakdown of the balance between freedom and authority930.

A service owed to society.

Its values and its demands.

Sacrament of intimate union with God.

b) The school. “The extreme importance of education in human life and its ever-growing influence on the social progress of this age”931.

The school, a social institution whose chief purpose is to set the human person on the way to integral formation, must be a community integrating all its components and in turn part of the local community and open to the national community; it must be dynamic and vital, ready for timely and sincere renewal, open to ecumenical dialogue and ready to make up for deficiencies found in the family environment932.

With these new perspectives on the school, a new educational landscape can already be glimpsed in every social setting, or at least such awareness has been reached that everyone is working hard to find solutions to the anguishing problem of the age: the education of the new generations; a problem made ever more urgent and vital by the climate of protest and rebellion which, born within the family because of the breakdown of the balance between authority and freedom, is spreading ever more worryingly to the school as well.

c) The Church. The Church holds the saving powers received from her Founder933. In carrying out her task, “the Church is not motivated by an earthly ambition but is interested in one thing only: to carry forward the work of Christ under the lead of the befriending Spirit, who came into the world to bear witness to the truth, to rescue and not to sit in judgment, to serve and not to be served”934. Therefore “nothing genuinely human fails to raise an echo in her heart”935. From this follows “the duty, at all times, of scrutinizing the signs of the times and of interpreting them in the light of the Gospel, so that, in language intelligible to each generation, she can respond to the perennial questions people ask about this present life and the life to come, and about the relationship of the one to the other”936.

The great upheavals, transformations and advances of the contemporary world change not only people's way of life but also their thinking937 and consequently their religious attitude, so that while on the one hand it is purified “of a magical view of the world and of superstitions that still circulate, and demands day by day a more personal and explicit adherence to faith... many regard the denial of God or of religion... as a requirement of scientific progress”938.

Thus we see that perennial values are interpreted in a very relative way. This explains the serious phenomenon of desacralization the world is undergoing today, which has very grave effects on the world of youth.

The problems of youth

16. At this historical moment, interesting but difficult in every field, young people face a whole range of new problems that provoke many conflicts between generations939; “conflicts that call for a sincere effort of understanding and dialogue on the part of both young people and adults”940.

It is therefore necessary to welcome young people “with trust and love”941, remembering that their attitudes express the times and that, while on the one hand they herald values that renew history, these are unfortunately accompanied by the denial of other great values942.

Concretely, we can find the following characteristics in today's youth:

a) Authenticity and sincerity. A demand rooted in the scientific and technical spirit of the present age, which makes young people more sensitive to the witness of life than to words and institutionalized norms.

This realism leads them to demand that in every sector of life and every activity, and especially in religious matters, all human values be taken into account and duly appreciated.

This highly positive value is, however, exposed to the influence of an arbitrary interpretation and judgment of reality, as well as to the demand for quick solutions, both negative attitudes which, besides causing them anguish and dissatisfaction, drive them to rebel against the “passivity” of adults and existing structures943.

b) Capacity to adapt to new situations. In a world immersed in exceptional dynamism, young people show a great capacity to adapt, which makes them sensitive to every new situation and open to receiving new values, with the consequent danger, given the prevailing relativism, of a lack of principles that would compromise an accurate assessment of events and authentic values and could also degenerate into a rejection of the whole heritage of the past and of existing social structures, almost wanting to build a new world in a highly idealistic vision944.

c) A sense of solidarity. The process of socialization in today's society makes “youth particularly sensitive to social problems and consequently more open to a pluralistic society and a more universal dimension of fellowship”945.

This sense of solidarity, faced with human injustice, drives them to defend trampled rights with an attitude that can go as far as violence946.

d) A longing for community life. One of the great changes in humanity today is the growing demand for community life in all spheres of human activity.

Young people, who already breathe this community atmosphere and long for the emotional security they rarely find in the family today, show themselves positively open to friendship, dialogue and group work, even though “in turn they run the risk of closing themselves into small aggressive groups”947.

e) A tendency toward personalization and self-assertion. Today more than ever, young people are aware “of the exalted dignity proper to the human person, since he stands above all things, and his rights and duties are universal and inviolable”948. This self-discovery as persons leads young people to assert their freedom, often excessively.

Human dignity and freedom, values inherent in the human condition, are extolled with great enthusiasm by all young people in a search for total independence that causes many tensions in relations with authority and can also degenerate into a selfish assertion of their rights.

This whole complex of positive values and negative attitudes characterizing today's young woman subjects her being and existence to pressures and tensions that significantly affect her emotional life.

That is why, in response to the longing for sincerity young people show, our work must be a continual and loving call “to a constant deepening of their authenticity and to self-criticism of their shortcomings”949, a call to be made in an attitude of open and sincere dialogue, through which the young woman can recognize the permanent values that “lead her to fulfill herself through gradual choices aimed at practicing Gospel values,” authentically lived950.

17. From all that has been said in the introductory exposition emerges the need to take the whole reality described into account, not only as a theoretical starting point but also as a practical viewpoint, both when examining and recognizing vocations and in setting up and carrying out the work of formation in its various stages.

Given the characteristics of today's young women, it is essential to establish norms and conditions that are not rigid but realistic and practical, which, while safeguarding the permanent values of religious life and the unity of the Institute, can be adapted to different regions, so that new members, as young shoots of the Congregation, may grow and bear fruits of salvation in the Church of God.

A) Conditions of suitability

Examination of vocations.

18. The Religious Vocation, a gift of divine grace granted to some by the Father951, must be examined and recognized through the signs the Lord uses every day to make his will known to prudent Christians952. Signs that must be considered and that require a work of accompaniment and selection which, following God's voice, fosters the candidate's free, personal and mature decision, while ensuring as far as possible her suitability for our Congregation.

Mother Rosa acted no differently, as Fiocchi states: “She wanted to know people well before opening the doors of the religious house to them; the information had to be detailed, documented and fully satisfactory”953.

Age

So that the young candidate may offer the assurance and capacity to take on a free and conscious commitment before God and others, as religious life requires, it is considered appropriate to set a minimum age of 18.

Human maturity

Clearly, anyone who feels called to a vocation of consecration to God in a mission of service to others needs human maturity as an indispensable basis that in some way guarantees both the development of her personality and the effectiveness of her future apostolate, while recognizing the value of grace, which always acts by elevating nature. In this regard it must be stressed that certain personality defects—selfishness, insincerity, stubbornness, a spirit of contradiction—are contraindicated for Community life, since, just as they harm personal growth, they hinder the dynamics of community.

Maturity, moreover, will always be relative. This means that in judging a candidate's maturity, the environment she comes from should be taken into account, and with this in mind three central areas of personality should be explored:

1. intellectual ability;

2. psycho-affective structure and character;

3. health and physical condition.

To this end, “...their physical and mental fitness should be investigated, using also the precise anamnestic and diagnostic judgment of an expert physician, with attention also to possible hereditary defects, especially mental ones”954.

The candidate for religious life:

- must have normal intelligence and a minimum level of education corresponding to compulsory schooling, preferably not below secondary studies;

- must enjoy good physical and mental health;

- must come from a healthy family environment.

These conditions will be the basis for judging the degree of human maturity, whose main criteria are:

- a certain stability of spirit;

- the ability to make decisions;

- the ability to judge people and events soundly.

In some cases it will be necessary not only to verify the existence of this maturity but also to complete it955.

Christian maturity

Christian maturity is a process that involves one's whole life and will be fully realized only in the bosom of the Father. Meanwhile, all of us, through personal effort and helped by the grace at work in us, must attain “the measure of the full stature of Christ”956.

That is why the young woman, in her first stage toward maturity, will regard Christianity as essential for her happiness and personal fulfillment, and will feel the longing to move from a merely passive and conventional adherence to the faith to a more active involvement in the ecclesial community.

It makes the vocational dialogue authentic.

Hers is still an imperfect and fragmentary knowledge of the unity “that exists between God's saving plan, accomplished in Christ, and human aspirations; between the Church, the People of God, and temporal communities; between God's revealing action and human experience; between supernatural gifts and charisms and human values”957; as this knowledge matures, it will lead her in time to a conscious and free choice of her mission, taken up within the Church and in the service of humanity958. Consequently, the candidate:

- must have a clear idea of her call to a life of faith;

- must be willing to live her baptismal consecration in a specific vocation;

- must be aware of her responsibility in God's creating and sustaining plan, mindful that her mission of service is a commitment to the Father and to the Christian community, a commitment requiring generous self-giving.

Religious sensitivity959

1) Spiritual life in general:

- a need for prayer,

- attraction to the things of God,

- a spirit of sacrifice.

“Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is from God, so that we may understand the gifts bestowed on us by God”960.

Mother Rosa, who in the early days reserved to herself the acceptance of postulants, was very demanding on this point and “did not want people who were content with ordinary virtue but required the resolve to reach a high degree of holiness: “For,” she said, “such is the Lord's will in taking us out of the world”961.

2) Inclination toward the Institute's own apostolic activities:

Another requirement, very much alive in Mother Rosa's mind from the beginning, was suitability for our works. In the first Regulation, when setting out the norms for acceptance, she says: “provided they are moved by the desire to consecrate themselves to God and to the service of the poor sick”962.

In identifying the candidate's religious sensitivity, however, one must consider that today she has a very particular view of religion and of the things of God, as was noted in the earlier study on the problems of youth and the world situation.

Since apostolic inclination and interest in one's surroundings are today inherent in the youthful spirit, it is clearly important to discern in the candidate:

- traces of an experience of encounter with Christ, to whom she wishes to consecrate herself with undivided love;

- moral certainty of fulfilling her vocation in our Institute963.

These first signs, as they develop, will lead her to total and definitive self-giving to Christ in a mission of service.
