of a call to religious life.

Formation: Sign and Demand.

Although this call from God can be discovered and lived personally only in progressive stages, the decisive role of the hierarchical ministry is evident:

- at its beginning and during its development, through the work of fostering vocations; although this is the task of the whole Christian community, it is up to the Bishops966 and Priests967 to give the necessary impetus. The Priest, by his ministry, is the direct mediator of God's call; hence at this stage spiritual direction is of the greatest importance, guiding the young people it considers suitable968 to become aware of the gift God has given them and, with absolute respect for their personality, helping them give a generous response to the divine call, always fostering a free and conscious choice.

- Finally, it is the hierarchical Church that, “by virtue of the authority given her by God, receives the vows of those professing them; by her public prayer she begs aid and grace from God for them... associating their self-offering with the Eucharistic sacrifice”969.

B) Formation for religious life

Purpose of formation

20. Formation, a basic and decisive factor in the whole life of the Congregation and an indispensable condition for the renewal called for by the Council970, must set itself the final goal of forming:

- Authentic personalities, that is, responsible and autonomous, able to strive every day to be “conformed to the image of the Son,” the goal God in his plan has set for every person971.

- Deeply motivated by love, that is, having reached in their personal relationship with God a friendship whose deepest expression is mutual trust and self-giving: “Those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them”972.

- Aware of their mission, sure of having been called within the ecclesial community to consecrate themselves totally to God, living charity in the service of others and so contributing “to implanting and strengthening the kingdom of Christ in souls and to spreading it to every land”973.

- Committed to their specific vocation as Daughters of Saint Anne, that is, well-defined Christian personalities who, having discovered their vocation, docile to the action of the Spirit, live it with enthusiasm, aware that their human possibilities will always be enhanced by the charism974.

Understood in this way, religious formation presents itself as both a sign and a demand.

A sign of God's Will, which seeks to lead the religious, as a consecrated woman, to the full realization of her baptismal commitment.

A demand that requires those responsible for formation not only to review methods but first of all to reflect on the being of the young woman to be formed, set within the moment in which she is called to live and work.

Hence the need to begin studying the problem of formation with a vision that places it not so much on the level of renewing methods as, above all, on the level of clarifying principles whose reasons spring from considering Creation itself.

Fundamental principles of formative action

An organic conception of the universe.

21. Sacred Scripture presents the Universe to us as a reality that arose at the creative call of God; of this God who, one and transcendent, gives created things a consistency, a truth and a foundation of their own and, at the same time, shapes them into an order that manifests his Omnipotence and Wisdom. God, Cause and Lord of the Universe, leads it to its perfection not immediately but through the secondary causes that he himself established […] give created reality an autonomy whose laws and values man must discover, use and order by virtue of the divine command.

God's action through creatures.

God governs irrational creatures by natural laws, but to man, made in His image and endowed with intelligence and will, he makes known in various ways what he wants him to do, using creatures too to show him his will and help him carry it out; man's response will be the free acceptance of this will, and in obedience to it he will find his full realisation. This shows us how the whole dynamic of growth is centred on God, but mediately. The way to God is therefore co-ordinated through creatures; and so, ultimately, formation and education [are] the action of God, who makes use of secondary causes to bring man «to the same end, [that is, to] Him».975

Formation: growth within a Community.

An organic conception of the human person

Formation: harmony between nature and grace.

22. In its simple narrative, Genesis presents the unity of body and soul that constitutes the essence of the human being: man, by his bodily reality, is a synthesis of the material universe; by his interiority, the image of God, he is superior to the whole universe, because he is capable of knowing and loving his Creator through free acceptance of divine friendship.

God's creative will established this harmony between body and soul, nature and grace; a harmony that, broken by sin, was restored by Christ, who through his redeeming work freed and strengthened humanity, renewing it inwardly, raising it up and perfecting it976.

This integral view of the human person, redeemed in Christ, leads us to conclude that all formative action, respecting the order willed by God, must integrate both aspects, nature and grace, so that all the person's fundamental predispositions and tendencies—conscious, subconscious and unconscious—are permeated by faith and love. Only thus will the whole person contribute to the personal encounter with God.

Preserving this harmony between nature and grace leads to the formation of an authentically Christian personality.

An organic conception of society

23. The human person, created in the image and likeness of God, One and Three, is by inner nature a social being who can neither live nor develop his or her qualities without relating to others977.

To be a person means to be open to the other, to enrich and be enriched, and in a relationship of love to build a “WE,” that is, a communion. A community of persons that Christian Revelation will relate to the very mystery of God: “That they may be one, as we are one”978.

“This likeness reveals that man... cannot fully find himself except through a sincere gift of himself”979.

Therefore it is through one's conduct, in mutual service and dialogue, that social life enhances the person and enables him or her to respond to their vocation980.

The fundamental law of formation: fidelity to human reality.

God reveals his will in the nature of beings.

Hence the need for formation, responding to the social instinct the human person possesses as God's image, to help shape his or her personality, fostering harmonious growth within a community which, in the diversity of persons, tends toward the unity of love.

C) The subject of formation

24. All the foregoing considerations show that the order of being determines the order of action.

Hence the need to know reality as it presents itself, for in it the Creator has engraved his Will.

Speaking of formation, one can say that the only valid pattern is that of life itself; to enter into it, we must therefore consider:

- the human being

- the individual person

- the historical context.

The human being

25. Starting from the principle of the organic conception of the human person, which shows its integral reality, we think it necessary to complete this vision, and once again we find our guide in the words of Genesis: “God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them”981.

The image of God is thus embodied in two modes: man and woman. Equal, because of the same nature, they are nonetheless different, because their structure, function and tasks will differ (cf. Gen 2:21-23).

In this regard, and concretely in our case, we will consider four aspects in the subject of formation:

- her dimension as a conscious and free person

- her developmental dimension

- her mission

- her femininity,

and for greater usefulness we will add their practical application.

a) The human person, conscious and free

In the hierarchy of created beings, the human person has a dignity that brings him closer to God than any other being: the capacity for self-determination: “God willed to leave man in the power of his own counsel”982. That is, the person holds his destiny in his hands and can fulfill himself and direct himself to his end by virtue of rational insight and free decision.

The decisive value of freedom for the personalization and sanctification of the human person requires us to examine its reality and consequences more deeply983.

This freedom, which on the divine level is conditioned by God's creative and saving will, on the human level tends to free the person from slavery to the passions through sincere acceptance of oneself with one's qualities and defects, and through acceptance of and respect for both contingent situations and the demands of interdependence and communion with others.

Pedagogical applications

1) Those responsible for formation, out of the respect due to the dignity and rights of the human person, must have a clear vision of the Truth and Values they are called to communicate.

They must therefore:

- give a precise, orderly and living knowledge of revealed truths, teaching how to distinguish in religious practice what is essential from what is contingent;

- establish an orderly hierarchy of values and present them in a synthesis suited to the ideal of the Daughters of Saint Anne, so as to stimulate and help the shaping of personality. They must also:

2) foster self-formation, based on a pedagogy of encouragement and genuine dialogue that spurs convinced adherence and generous, constant and free self-giving to Christ and his Church.

This pedagogical method presupposes a systematic education in freedom, that is:

- in the correct understanding of religious obedience, which consists in the richness of Christian freedom, reaching its perfection in the self-offering of the person to God through Faith984;

- in teaching how to distinguish falsely free behavior, that is, capricious and inconstant, the fruit of immaturity, from responsible behavior, the fruit of authentic inner freedom;

- in gradually accustoming them to act on their own initiative, entrusting real responsibilities and helping them acquire the ability to make decisions, even at the risk of possible failures. The formative value of mistakes must never be forgotten;

- in encouraging co-responsibility in building the community of prayer, work and recreation.

3) Formation so directed will lead the Daughter of Saint Anne:

- to set her life within the perspective of an organic world of truths and values which, while giving an accurate view of reality, communicates security, support and stability;

- to avoid getting lost in insignificant details that distort the image of God and of religious life;

- to educate herself responsibly, learning to master the reality within which she must pursue her path to holiness.

Feeling truly free will give the Daughter of Saint Anne the joy of her obedience in the fullness of dedication to God.

b) The human person in her developmental dimension

Growth, whether physiological, psychological or spiritual, must lead the person to acquire a personality all the more authentic the higher the goal set: that of the complete human being, “to the measure of the full stature of Christ”985, for “whoever follows Christ, the perfect man, becomes himself more of a man”986.

This growth, however, presupposes a slow and gradual conquest through daily experience and the constant help of Grace, both because the human person is in himself a contingent and finite creature and because, though endowed with the intellectual and volitional capacities needed to reach human maturity, he finds himself in the condition of fallen nature.

The duty and need for this perfecting must be felt more keenly by the religious called to carry out a mission as a “sign” in the ecclesial community, because “God's love has been poured into her heart and urges her on according to the measure of grace she has received”987.

Pedagogical applications

1) The human person is always capable of greater perfection; therefore formation:

- must not be limited to certain periods but must be a continuous, lifelong commitment;

- must make use of the human tendency toward self-improvement, presenting authentic values so that, by personal acceptance, she may realize them in her life.

2) Formation must give the Church Daughters of Saint Anne capable of giving their lives to God while responding to the needs of the world they live in, and this implies an integral and specific education according to each one's particular mission, carried out continuously.

3) This constant updating will enable the Daughter of Saint Anne:

- to give, with assurance, a faithful response to her vocation: a dialogue with God that demands conversion of life and commitment to others;

- to feel herself a contemporary of a world in tension and continual change, while being a sign of unchanging values;

- to keep faith in life and retain the capacity to rejoice in humanity's continual development, remembering that she herself is consecrated to the God who gladdens her perennial youth.

c) The human person in her mission

The human person, able to know and love the Creator, finds the highest reason for his or her dignity in the vocation to communion with God988, the God who, truly Personal in the dynamic of the Trinity, created us as persons in order to “be together.” For human beings this “being together” means a communication of love on two distinct and complementary planes: a vertical one involving participation in God's saving plan, “being toward the Father,” and a horizontal one involving dialogue with humanity, the People of God, “being toward one's brothers and sisters,” because “love of God and neighbor is the first and greatest commandment.”

From this follows for the human person a vocation to mission, to be carried out within the Church, the Sacrament of Christ, in an attitude of faith, hope and love:

- Faith to discern the sign of God's presence in events and in people's lives;

- Hope to inspire him in building the world in the perspective of the Kingdom;

- Love to make him one with all people989.

Pedagogical applications

If every person is called to a mission in the Church, for us this mission takes concrete form in consecration to God according to the charism proper to the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Therefore, in its practical application, formation:

1) Must be imbued with awareness of our charism, so that knowledge of our spirituality and the fulfillment of the mission God has entrusted to us as Daughters of Saint Anne are two converging lines. This requires:

- being faithful to the past, entering into Mother Rosa's spirit and discovering in the great moments of grace in our history the divine initiative that gave origin and life to the “Work of God”;

- being faithful to the present, seeking to discover God's voice in events, because he continually renews his call.

2) This dynamic formation, rooted in our particular charism, will enable each Daughter of Saint Anne:

- to grow and renew her spirit in fulfilling the mission God has entrusted to the Congregation;

- to feel herself an active member of the Work of God.

And so, faithful to our own identity, we will be formed as religious in love with our vocation and imbued with our ideal as Daughters of Saint Anne.

d) The feminine being

God creates the human being in his image and likeness, and in this likeness God makes:

- man the embodiment of his Wisdom and Power, image of the Son;

- woman the embodiment of his Love, image of the Holy Spirit, who is receptivity and self-giving.

Femininity, springing thus from the depths of her being as a woman, cannot be reduced merely to physiological differentiation; it contains a whole wealth of psychological and spiritual values that give woman the capacity to be, within humanity, the embodiment of love in the fundamental balance of her personality. A balance achieved in the creative tension of two poles:

- that of virginity, expressed in her attitude of delicate and intimate reserve;

- that of motherhood, revealed in her serving and welcoming self-giving.

Feminine tendencies can be summed up as:

A tendency toward interiority and spirituality. Woman experiences herself above all as soul and tends to give life to what is bodily. In carrying out her mission she “does things with her heart,” leaving her mark on everything.

A tendency toward self-giving. By her very nature woman longs for and seeks wholeness in the gift of herself, and in this gift, because of her affective richness, she needs self-forgetfulness. Hers is a gift to a person rather than to a work or a task; consequently she always seeks a “YOU” to whom to devote herself in an attitude of receptive self-offering and service.

A tendency toward purity, shown in woman's characteristic modesty as a natural protection of her being and her mission.

This brief view of the feminine being would not be complete without considering her special situation in this age, which tends toward the advancement of women: “The hour is coming, in fact has come, when the vocation of women is being achieved in its fullness, the hour in which women acquire in the world an influence, an effect and a power never hitherto achieved”990.

These words reveal to us not only a full liberation of women but also the whole set of problems involved in their integration into present-day society. An integration which, if it starts from a distorted and un-Christian view of the feminine being, often runs the risk of distancing woman from the mission God has assigned her.

Today more than ever she, as the embodiment of love, must show and ensure that love regains its true meaning, “reconciling people with life”991.

Pedagogical applications

1) Formation must be oriented in the perspective of the feminine being, grasping its originality so as to lead it to the fullness of its maturity and its virginal self-offering. This implies:

- presenting the feminine ideal clearly;

- leading the religious to live the ideal of her Consecration in a total gift of exclusive belonging to Christ through living her vows;

- developing the feminine values of order, cleanliness and good taste, giving the religious the opportunity to show her personal initiative in carrying them out;

- grasping the expression of her delicacy and virginal interiority so as to bring it to fullness as an expression of true modesty and reserve: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God”992;

Knowing the person, who is one and unique.

Considering the human person in the reality of his time.

- cultivating the tendency to self-denial, shown in small services and in renouncing small and great satisfactions out of love;

- gradually awakening in her the sense of spiritual motherhood, which reaches its fullness in the apostolic mission.

2) This education must reach the unconscious and the subconscious; it therefore requires:

- a supernatural atmosphere based on human and feminine balance;

- those directly responsible for formation, Superiors and Mistresses, must embody the values inherent in the ideal of consecration;

- conforming the religious to Mary, Daughter of Saint Anne, the ideal figure of woman fulfilled in her deepest and highest aspirations: Virgin, Bride and Mother.

3) Consequently, interiorization along the line of being leads:

- to confidence and self-possession, shown in unreserved self-giving, aware both of the great possibilities and of the limitations of feminine nature;

- to the security of feeling personally loved by God and the certainty that her life has meaning and an effectiveness always possible, despite struggles and moments of discouragement.

Finally, this immersion of the religious in the truth of her being will be the source of her freedom, for as the Lord said: “The truth will make you free”993.

The individual person

26. Attentive listening to the voice of each individual is a necessary condition for recognizing and defining a society, which will be the more effective the more each of its members is truly himself or herself.

A person is truly herself only to the extent of her fidelity to the personal vocation to which God has called her, giving her at the same time the necessary grace and ability994, without forgetting that the deep voice of this personalization is love understood as the gift of self.

This fidelity and originality in response will give each person's life and history an unrepeatable structure.

Pedagogical applications

Formative action must be carried out with respect for the mystery of each person, who is one and unique. This requires of those responsible for formation:

- listening in order to discover God's Voice regarding each person, that is, seeking to know her by discovering all the good in this “YOU” in the making, and accepting her as she is;

- helping her fulfill herself through honest acceptance of her gifts and limitations and of the immense possibilities grace offers her;

- leading her to find in love the strength and motive for her self-giving, so that through her growth the whole community may reach its goal;

- offering her the possibility of feeling secure, useful and personally loved.

This formation, which we may call liberating, will help each Daughter of Saint Anne to enter into the depths of her own “I,” to know herself and to go beyond the limits of natural selfishness. And so she will reach her ideal: to achieve in poverty the living synthesis of the one love in its twofold dimension: God and neighbor.

The historical context

27. If we wish to understand the human person fully, we must think of him as a BEING who is gradually fulfilled in the world and with the world, with others and with God.

Daughter of Saint Anne: committed to her own fulfillment through Mother Rosa's charism.

This fulfillment in time gives rise to a dialectical tension between the person, who transforms the world in the work of personalization, and the world, which, as a reality in continual evolution, conditions the person's action and very being; a dialectic that ends only when the person has reached in Charity “the full stature of Christ”995, the supreme end of human dignity. So understood, perfection in charity presupposes:

- recognition by the human person of the goodness of the laws and values of transitory things that divine Wisdom created for the benefit of our life and holiness996;

- dialogue with others to read the signs of the times and fittingly incorporate these values into human activity, illuminating them with the light of the Gospel so as to free them and refer them to the Savior's dominion997.

Pedagogical applications

1) Formation must be able to touch and channel the living soul of the historical moment in which we are called to live. This implies:

- discovering and grasping the ways today's young woman thinks, feels and reacts;

- fostering at every moment a relationship with the universal Good and Truth revealed in the events of history and of life.

2) It is necessary to direct formation “toward an adult personal faith, interiorized, active and constantly measured against present-day life, especially in this time of transition”998.

For the religious this implies:

- an interiorization of the Word of God that will enable her to discover in personal prayer the divine initiative in her own life;

- active participation in the Mystery of Faith: Mass and Liturgy;

- a commitment to learning to discern God's plans and will through world, Church, national, community and personal events.

3) In this way formation, while becoming sensitive to the world's currents that condition its pedagogical action, will enable the religious:

- to dialogue with the world while remaining faithful to herself and her vocation;

- to seek in prayer the right interpretation of the “signs of the times,” of the demands of today's world and of what God personally asks of her;

- to avoid the exaggerated exaltation of human values and the pursuit of power, wealth, pleasure and success proper to “the world.”

The religious will thus be able to bear witness to a total and full human and religious existence, the words of the Gospel being fulfilled in her: “You are the salt of the earth”999; “you are in the world, but not of the world”1000.

D) Formation: a lifelong commitment

28. All these reflections, with their practical applications, tell us that formation must answer the existential question of our life as Daughters of Saint Anne, seeking to cooperate with divine grace as fittingly as possible in shaping authentic women who, consecrated to God in the Church of this time and living our charism, are able to fire all the faithful with enthusiasm for winning the Kingdom.

To achieve this means making formation the principal commitment of one's whole life.

However, the strength of this supernatural impulse, which every Daughter of Saint Anne must experience, can be obtained only through a life rooted in one's charism.

Personal responsibility.

At every moment the image of Mother Rosa must be for us a living and close memory. She was the depositary of the “gift” God made to our Family, and it was to her that he entrusted “His Work.”

Her presence among us, therefore, cannot be only a memory that rekindles filial affection; above all it must mean fidelity to the Lord, because it is in her teachings and her life that we will find clear guidance on the Divine Will that wished to raise up in the Church the Family of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

This close contact with our Mother's spirit will undoubtedly renew the wonderful effects her presence produced at the dawn of the foundation, as can be seen from the quotation reported by Fr. Fiocchi: “After my conversation with her (Rosa) I can no longer resist; I feel the Lord wants me in her Institute”1001.

The meaning of self-formation

29. Formation understood in this way, as a lifelong commitment, will find no echo in the life of the Daughter of Saint Anne unless it is directed toward responsible self-formation.

The human person is responsible and “the artisan of his own success or failure”1002; no one can or should entrust his life to others' decisions. The religious too, although she finds a sure guide in obedience, precisely because true obedience is free and liberating, must shape most of her life herself through dialogue with others and with the events of history.

Continuous self-formation will give the religious the fullness of her consecration and the effectiveness of her mission.

All formative action must therefore awaken in the Daughter of Saint Anne a sense of duty and personal responsibility for formation; to this end she must be offered:

- a Community in which the sense of friendship and shared ideals create a warm family atmosphere;

- a central idea that will be the point of reference for evaluating her actions: the idea of belonging to the “Work of God,” set within the Church as a “sign” of love for humanity;

- a Head, a Person who with absolute value makes the solution of every problem possible: Christ, the Crucified;

- a Model: Mary, Virgin Mother, humble Servant of the Lord, the embodied ideal of the Daughter of Saint Anne;

- a Guide: Saint Anne, Mother of Mary;

- a Figure: Mother Rosa, the full realization of our vocation;

- a commitment: the conquest of love, the choice of her own role in continuing the mystery of the poverty of Christ, sent by the Father to proclaim the Good News to the poor;

- humble and sincere acceptance of her natural gifts, her limitations and the concrete situations in which God places her;

- an attitude of deep faith that lets divine grace act freely, giving human nature, elevated by it, the confidence to advance joyfully on the way of charity;

- the enrichment and updating, day by day, of her spiritual, doctrinal and professional culture, intelligently selecting and assimilating all that is offered to her—study courses, conferences, etc.—and her contacts with the work in which she is engaged, with society and with the world;

- open availability to the demands of today's world and of the Church, to the cultural conditions and mentality of the environment in which she works, because building the new Kingdom does not mean destroying the old but integrating it in a balanced way, since Christ came not “to abolish the law... but to fulfill it”1003.

Community responsibility.

Continuing formation at this point is extremely active and responsible; it is the time when work springs from the maturity already acquired and nourishes the development of a personality that has to its credit the fruit of countless experiences1004.

Thanks to this demanding work, the religious will be able to take a leading place in the Christian community and bear witness to all of the wonderful effectiveness of Christ's Kingdom and the infinite power of the Holy Spirit, who works wonders in the Church1005.

The dynamic Community

30. Precisely because she does not renounce being a woman, the religious feels the need to love and be loved, and therefore community life is the most suitable response to these feminine needs, while also giving her the opportunity for healthy self-control.

It is precisely in this fraternal encounter that the religious, oriented in her first years of formation toward a pedagogy of freedom, gradually perfects her personality, and in this work, while exerting the influence of her personality on the other members, she is influenced by them.

The religious community, becoming thus the “Sacrament of Unity” of its members with one another and with God, a union that finds its highest expression in community prayer and especially in the Eucharistic celebration1006, here takes on its most important aspect: that deriving from its responsibility as a forming community.

Hence the formative importance of true friendship and community fellowship which, animated by faith, hope and charity, will enable us to overcome every obstacle, renew our enthusiasm and send us into the world as authentic apostles of the Gospel.

Only in this atmosphere of community fellowship and mutual friendship can each religious acquire two fundamental elements of her consecration: security and fidelity.

This security is founded on the theological virtues, by which, overcoming false notions of humility that limit the development of one's human values, the religious accepts herself in her concrete situation and in understanding encounter with the ideas, thoughts, gifts and faults of her sisters, and while fully realizing herself, actively cooperates in the realization of the others.

The difficult moments and crises that inevitably occur in religious life too can jeopardize fidelity to commitment if they do not meet with the fraternal understanding of the community; when they do, they become a rich source of growth, especially in affective maturity.

To be faithful to their consecration, which is a life of fervent charity for the good of all the people, religious, in conforming themselves to the Christ of the Gospel, cannot fail to be profoundly distinct from the human environment in which they live; a distinction that is not separation, indifference, fear or contempt, but dialogue with the world in which they have been placed as a sign and witness.

In this encounter they will receive influences that will contribute considerably to their formation.

Indeed, in relationships outside the community, whether formal, such as study courses and conferences, or occasional, through apostolic contact with lay people or other religious, as well as through public opinion and the various media of social communication, each religious will find a source of knowledge that will contribute to her own growth to the extent that she is properly prepared and set on the path of personalized formation.

Negative influences.

31. This does not exclude the danger of possible negative influences, which the community must not only not ignore but forestall, remembering that only in the consistency of an authentically religious life is there the strength that gives immunity “from the contagion of the surrounding human misery and from the seduction of the equally surrounding human splendor”1007.

A community that supports.

In practical terms, the obligations and duties of the community as a whole and of the Superior as the one responsible for the group can be set out.

32. It is the Community's task:

1) To guarantee, through mutual respect and help, the balance each religious must strive for, valuing each one's gifts and fostering as much as possible the exchange of intellectual, cultural and moral riches.

2) To foster, as Mother Rosa wished, that unity of heart which makes each a sharer in the Paschal Mystery, relaxes the spirit, brightens the atmosphere and fosters liberation from all that belongs to the “old self,” so that the “new self” may grow1008.

3) To commit itself responsibly to making use of all the means and opportunities offered, occasionally or formally, to increase its spiritual, doctrinal and professional culture, in harmony with the development and esteem of human values and the needs of time and place.

4) To adapt to the needs of the ecclesial community; an adaptation which in turn means adjusting to the demands apostolic work imposes on each religious, and therefore setting, by common agreement, a suitable timetable so as not to fail in observing a just and prudent religious discipline1009.

5) In a word, to live one's consecration consciously, sure that only thus will the light of good example shine before all, an irresistible attraction even in the darkness of silence.

The Superior will have the particular obligation to foster, “according to each one's intellectual abilities and personal character...,” their participation in courses of further training and updating, conferences, etc., of a spiritual and cultural nature, whether organized by the Congregation, by the Conferences of Religious, by lay people or by the State, and to provide them with the necessary resources, particularly a suitably updated and easily accessible library1010.

Without forgetting that, as the one responsible for a group that has chosen total consecration to God as its goal, her first and most important task will be to animate and foster the inner life of all, especially through liturgical life, so that in personal encounter with Christ each Sister may find the light, strength and love that assure her an authentic incarnation in this increasingly secularized world.

Harmony and complementarity.

Unity of thought and action.

Introduction

The vocation of a Daughter of Saint Anne is lived concretely by a particular person, in her situation of time and place, in one of our communities. Personalization of the call and fulfillment in community are two complementary terms that require a structure which, grasping personal aspirations, coordinates and channels the mission1011 in harmony with the Congregation's own charism.

Clearly these structures, always necessary in common life, must be marked especially during the period of formation by their dynamism and flexibility, so that an effective education may lead to conscious and free responsibility, in the unceasing search for God and love of others, in order to bring the candidate to the “definitive choice” of being a Daughter of Saint Anne and to a life consistent with this vocation.

It is in this perspective that the structure of our formation cycle is studied.

A) The period of formation properly so called

33. The fact that formation must be a lifelong commitment does not lessen the importance of the period of formation properly so called, which runs from the candidate's admission to the Congregation until Perpetual Profession, for this is precisely the time of the gradual affirmation of her personality and of knowing and assimilating the great values of religious life. The fundamental requirement and principle of the whole formation cycle will be unity of thought and action: a unity which, by integrating, harmonizing and unifying the pedagogical efforts of each stage, leads the young woman to the free and conscious choice of being a Daughter of Saint Anne, rooted in its authentic values and lived as a personal response to God's call; this will lead her to unity of life, centered on one person alone: Christ1012.

34. In this sense of unity, formation presupposes:

1) Gradualness and progress:

- stage of preparation or Postulancy

- stage of initiation or Novitiate

- stage of deepening or Juniorate

2) Harmony and complementarity between:

- the objectives proper to the various stages, so that each, while fostering a particular aspect of formation, always keeps in view the fundamental unity of the whole educational process;

- the various elements that make up the integral formation of a Daughter of Saint Anne, so as to engage the whole person and every aspect of the person;

- theory and practice, so that formation may be seen as a vital need and a reality in which theoretical teaching is joined to practical activity, in contact with the ecclesial community and the social environment;

- prayer and action, as two expressions of a single vital reality: the supernatural love that unites the Daughter of Saint Anne with God, to whom she is consecrated, and with the people to whom she devotes herself, placing herself at their service.

God, the Educator par excellence.

Formation, an ecclesial function.

In harmony of spirit, heart and aims.

B) Factors of formation

Supernatural factors

a) God and his grace

35. The choice of religious life is the fruit of God's call and a response of faith. Consequently the first factor in the dynamic of formation is God himself, who calls his creatures and leads them toward a particular mission through his Spirit.

The unifying center of one's whole existence will therefore be faith in God, who calls and chooses solely because he loves; consequently the vocational choice will become ever more conscious as faith deepens and becomes in each one a living reality that engages her totally1013.

The search for God, an intimate and personal relationship with Christ, docility to the Spirit through prayer, participation in the Eucharistic mystery and sacramental life will be indispensable elements in the life of every future Daughter of Saint Anne. This will prepare her to become aware that her mission of service is solely the expression of the most authentic faith: faith in the call received from God for “His Work”; faith active in a “charity without limits and without reward”; faith that grows strong, in imitation of Saint Anne's, in meditation on the Word and in a familiar and constant relationship with the Father, through his Son Jesus Christ, in the Holy Spirit, as Mother Rosa lived1014.

b) Mary Most Holy and Saint Anne

36. Mary Most Holy, image of the woman fully realized in her deepest and highest aspirations, is the Daughter of Saint Anne who must be the model of our houses of formation.

Virgin and Mother of God and of the Church, she is the sublime embodiment of the ideal of woman and at the same time the humble servant of the Lord who, gathering in herself all the spirituality of the Old Testament, is identified with Christ the Redeemer in the mystery of his poverty.

It is in her, the Daughter of Saint Anne, that the young woman will learn to read her destiny and her greatness, understanding that her vocation associates her with that spirituality of the poor which in Mary and Saint Anne took on the specific meaning of a motherly presence.

The Church

37. The Church, sacrament of the encounter with God, is the vital space in which the various religious families are born, develop and grow. Having received the gifts of the evangelical counsels, she has the mission of helping those who feel called to discover them and to give a positive response, fulfilling their lives in a particular Congregation1015.

Formation is therefore founded on the Church's very mission and must be carried out in her name and with her spirit, awakening in the aspirant to religious life a deep union, dependence and love between her own life and mission and the life and mission of the Church. In our Congregation this union, springing from its own spirituality, is expressed as an act of fidelity to the charism received and to the action of the Spirit, who willed that the Daughters of Saint Anne be born in the Church as the fruit of an act of obedience to the Supreme Pontiff1016.

Those responsible for formation

38. Every religious vocation has its origin in a living encounter with the Lord, in a profound experience, and therefore at the root of the formation process we find God.

In this context, the educational action of those responsible for formation is nothing other than the help to take on an attitude of personal response to the call that each candidate has experienced in the depths of her being. The message they must hand on does not consist, therefore, in teaching to «do» but in leading to «be»; and so the outcome of formation work depends on the witness of life offered by the Superiors, the Mistresses and the members of the Community that has welcomed the aspirant. The close relation between the maturity of the candidate and the human and religious maturity of the Community is evident; hence the intimate union of spirit, heart and aims among those responsible for formation is indispensable: in the strictest sense of the word, they are all the members of a house in which a young woman is living one of the stages of formation: postulancy, novitiate, juniorate.

A spirituality of Advent.

Authority in relation to formation.

39. The success of formative work depends on the climate of affective relationships among the people of a house and in particular on the work of the Novice and Junior Mistresses: the formation of formators is therefore of fundamental importance, because it conditions the success of the Congregation and its future […].

A) The superiors

The superiors' task is to stimulate the integral growth of the candidate, with a formation attentive to her particular feminine sensitivity and at the same time in communion with the poor, the sick and the needy to whom she consecrates her whole life; it therefore requires an objective and enlightened knowledge of the actual situations of the surrounding environment.

According to the mind of the Council and the spirit of our Congregation, to exercise authority is above all to manifest the love with which God loves the sisters; being God's representatives means making visible one of the most delicate aspects of God's love: motherly love. Consequently, no authoritarianism, despotism or maternalism can have a place in the educational process, which aims to accustom young women in formation to the right use of freedom and to acting on their own initiative, thus gaining self-mastery so as to fulfill the plan in which God, in creating them, made them sharers1017.

40. This also requires that the Superior of the formation Community be a religious:

- imbued with the spirit of the Church and the spirit proper to the Daughters of Saint Anne;

- able to promote and maintain cohesion among the members in formation, the Mistresses and the professed sisters, so that they feel themselves a united Community fully committed, though in different ways, to the educational process;

- who knows the mentality of young women and is sensitive to their needs and problems, so as to help the Mistress in the process of their integration into the life of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

B) The mistresses

41. The present complexity of formation and the importance of the Community's influence mean that the Mistress is not solely responsible for formation; she must count on the collaboration of the Superior and the Community, as well as on the help of competent people. Nevertheless, it must be made clear that spiritual formation in the proper sense, in fidelity to the charism of the Congregation, given its profound character as the transmission and growth of life, is the specific task of the Mistress, who is to carry out this work in immediate dependence on the Superior Major.

1) Attitudes of the Mistress: instruments of God in the work of formation

2) Qualities of the Mistress: with particular qualities and specific aptitudes

42. The Mistress is the indispensable element in the formation process; she must commit herself totally to her task in order to give the educational encounter the active, vital and fruitful warmth that the formation of a religious requires.

Three fundamental qualities must mark her teaching: Love, Wisdom and Authority; qualities that ultimately derive from her position as God's representative in her educational work.

Love. Love is the attribute that sums up all the divine perfections. “God is love.” And it is love that leads people to the maturity of their full formation; therefore the Mistress's first function must be to love.

A supernatural love, expressed generously through affection, kindness, indulgence and interest; in a word, by exercising all the human virtues that characterize true love.

The Mistress's love must be liberating: it must elevate, encourage and sustain, reaching the depths of the self to help it overcome the limits of natural selfishness and lead it toward the goal of its ideal as a Daughter of Saint Anne. At the same time the Mistress, convinced that it is God who frees and elevates others, gently guides toward autonomy from the very beginning, knowing she must lead to personal maturity; yet, given the limits of human nature, just as the work of one's own perfection can never be called complete, so her task as guide can never be considered finished.

Wisdom. In God, Wisdom and Love are inseparable. God, who loves human beings, wishes to raise them to an existential knowledge of the truth that makes them free1018.

The Mistress, therefore, in her educational work, full of deep respect for the mystery of each person, will teach the young woman to discover and fulfill herself with her own abilities and characteristics, and will lead her to regard her whole being as a divine gift and the circumstances of her life as signs of God's saving action in her personal history.

In this way the young woman will gradually discover that the needs of her being find a response in the charism of religious life and in consecration to God.

Authority. God, as the author of life, is the only one who has rights over it. All authority proceeds from him, and the Mistress, because of her life-bearing mission, shares in this authority, which is essentially a service to life.

The Mistress's authority must aim at forming free and responsible personalities; she will therefore choose the educational means that most readily lead to the intended goal.

assist in formation.

Formation: the joint action of the whole Community.

43. The formation of new religious requires specific qualities in the Mistress.

Maturity. The Mistress's personality is the fundamental instrument of her pedagogical work; hence the need to free herself from every spirit of domination and capricious subjectivism, from infantilism and self-sufficiency. Only thus can she transcend herself and become capable of a fullness of virginal motherhood.

Magnanimity, made of self-denial and a spirit of sacrifice. Interest in the “you,” with breadth of vision, so as to grasp and welcome the concerns and questions of young people.

Motherly sensitivity, to choose wisely the means suited to winning, with simplicity and prudence, the young woman's trust, thus making it easier for her to open up and to wish to collaborate actively in her own formation.

Sufficient human preparation to keep abreast of contemporary culture, and specific knowledge of psychology, theology and the socio-economic situation of the environment.

A deep spirit of faith. It is impossible to educate for religious life without a deep sense of the supernatural and full conviction that it is God who works in souls and in everyday events.

An ecclesial spirit: the Mistress must be sensitive to the Church's concerns, know and share her anxieties, so as to lead young women to a universal and concrete openness to her needs and to the “full awareness that the hope of the Church and the salvation of souls are entrusted to them”1019.

The spirit of our Congregation. The ecclesial dimension of formation requires that the Mistress be imbued with the spirit of our Congregation, have a clear and loving knowledge of our spirituality and mission, and strive to be the living embodiment of the ideal God infused in Mother Rosa.

c) Collaborators

44. The need to give an integral formation requires the collaboration of specialized people: priests, religious and lay people who, in their respective fields, contribute as experts in the various aspects of formation, whether through regular courses, lectures or the sharing of experiences, etc. It goes without saying that they must be carefully chosen.

d) The forming Community

45. The aim of a forming community is the personal maturing of each of its members in keeping with the ends proposed by the Church and the Congregation.

Its effectiveness will therefore depend on its ability to help the young woman become an authentic religious, with all the inner transformations this implies, so that she in turn feels responsible for building up and maturing the Community itself.

In keeping with our origins, the Community is above all the Family of the Holy Mother, in which we fundamentally live the deep spiritual experience of our common self-giving to the love of God, in mutual consideration and in service of our neighbor.

So understood, the Community enters the dynamic of formation as a most important and irreplaceable factor, since it is in community experience that the candidate will assimilate in a living and practical way our own family spirit and our apostolic ideal.

Hence the need for the joint action of all the members of the Community, which, following the guidance given by the Mistress, must form an educational whole to form, in a climate of respect, openness and sincerity, those who will later become definitive members of our Congregation.

e) Confessors and spiritual directors

46. The vocation of a Daughter of Saint Anne, as openness and exclusive dedication to the Lord, requires a constant attitude of conversion, that is, of detachment from sin and renunciation of the world, in order to live a life hidden with Christ in God and to make continual progress on the way of charity and self-denial, which is the life of the Institute.

Such an attitude involves combat and struggle, in the midst of which, without outside help, one is not always able to discern the way of the Spirit with certainty; hence the need, as a valuable help, for the action of the spiritual director, which is of the utmost importance during the period of formation1020.

Respect for the intimacy of conscience and for the different ways by which the Spirit—the true guide to holiness—leads souls requires, with the greatest freedom, the presence of an experienced and prudent spiritual director with a sense of the Church and knowledge of our Institute's spirituality. Young women in formation will thus be offered sure guidance, especially at those moments of life when the whole human being appears to itself as an unsolved problem, perceived somewhat obscurely1021.

One aim only: the fulfillment of one's vocation in authenticity, freedom and immediate contact with life.

Formation community

47. The social dimension of the person and the teachings of Christ, who “founded, through the gift of his Spirit, a new fraternal communion,” are the human and supernatural foundation on which the religious Community is built, so as to manifest, through the union of brothers and sisters, the coming of Christ1022.

During the formation process this “union” must be the aim not only of the forming community but also of the young women in formation, so that, as a single body, they direct their efforts to the full realization of the law of love, which is the first Christian witness.

In this climate of true friendship, expressed in respect, trust, solidarity and concern for mutual help, it is easy to awaken in young women an awareness of the common goal: to build a true fraternal Community that helps each one to fulfill her personal vocation1023.

C) Means of formation

Houses of formation1024

48. Our young women, called by God to the Congregation, thirst for the absolute and at the same time ask—like all young people today—to take an active part in solving the world's problems1025.

For this tendency, wonderfully in keeping with the spirit of our Congregation, to be unified in a single supernatural love for God and for people, the period of formation must be spent in suitable settings that allow a deep encounter with the Lord and at the same time are organized so as to foster initiation into the future life of a Daughter of Saint Anne.

This necessarily implies that our Houses of formation, while offering the example of a life founded on authentic values, ask for an equally authentic response, so that their purpose is achieved in a climate of freedom, flexibility and immediate contact with life; in this way they will promote a personalizing education that will guide young women toward gradual personal choices aimed at the full realization of their vocation.

49. Consequently:

1) Houses of formation should be settings where the normal life of the Institute is lived, and they should be integrated into the local Church and the social reality of the country and the world.

2) Materially, the House should be open and welcoming, rich in the homely warmth that makes family life together easier for the group and helps form a community consciousness.

3) In keeping with our spirit of poverty, both luxury and deprivation should be avoided; marked by religious simplicity, the house must be provided with what is needed for the sisters' health and with the teaching aids necessary for their proper human, spiritual and apostolic formation.

4) The values of order, cleanliness and good taste must be cultivated, giving young women the opportunity to express their personal initiative in them.

Methods

50. In line with what was said earlier about the situation of young women in the contemporary world, and having already set out the fundamental principles and aim of our formative action, it is thought best not to formulate fixed norms or lay down particular educational methods. Instead, some practical guidelines are given, in keeping with a pedagogy of encouragement and with the spirit and purpose of our Congregation.

51. In general:

- Methods based on sincerity and love should express the shared desire, interest and commitment of those responsible and of the young women in formation to reach gradually the general and specific aim of each stage.

- Methods should be adapted to particular circumstances of time and place, so as to correspond to personal conditions and to the needs of the places where the young women are formed.

- Methods should be used that help the young woman develop her personal gifts in harmonious unity with her inner life and with a view to her entering a specific mission: “charity without limits and without reward, silent and hidden sacrifice”1026.

- Methods should be suitably tested and, if necessary, reworked according to the needs and capacity of the group in formation.

52. In particular:

- Suitable means should be used to create a lively, homely and dynamic atmosphere of evangelical simplicity and poverty, imbued with fraternal love and supernatural values.

Therefore:

- the house rule should aim to help personal freedom grow and to foster common life, giving security and never fear;

- the rules, few, strictly necessary and carefully weighed, should be firmly maintained;

- respect and trust, as a stimulus to all the good in each one, should be fostered to the utmost, excluding every method of distrust and surveillance;

- all formalism and everything that makes formation artificial should be avoided;

- the young woman should be guided, through the interiorization of the Word of God and active participation in the mystery of Faith (Mass and liturgy, personal prayer and reflection on the events and circumstances of her own life), to achieve ever more clearly the synthesis of her life in the Person of Christ.

53. The ideals that inspire our religious family should be presented in a way that engages every aspect of the aspirant's personality, bearing in mind the Gospel, the spirituality of the Institute and the present historical moment. Consequently:

- On the intellectual level, a clear and deep knowledge should be sought:

of the “sequela Christi,” as imitation of Christ chaste, poor and obedient;

of the Vocation of a Daughter of Saint Anne, as participation, within the Church, in the mystery of the poverty of Christ and Mary, in a form of motherly self-giving;

of the person and spirituality of Mother Rosa: through Christ, to the Father, in the Holy Spirit and in the heart of the Church;

of the spiritual heritage of the Institute and its traditions;

of the Constitutions and the Directories;

of the apostolic needs of the Congregation at the present time.

- On the affective level

liberating dialogue

respecting the dynamic of growth

Without undue pressure, respecting the principle of gradualness and the psychological and spiritual receptivity of each one, those responsible should strive to embody in their own lives the religious values they have undertaken to instill in the young women, so that they themselves may be a living and effective witness to the ideal lived in its fullness and in fulfilling its demands; that is, in a living, active and fruitful way.

- On the level of the will

The young woman's personal activity should be encouraged, so that, discovering these values for herself, she may value them inwardly, love them and, making them the ideal of her life, act consistently with them.

54. The demands of truth in formation require that it take place in open and sincere dialogue, since its aim is the “following” of the God of Truth.

Consequently, education should take place not so much through general instructions as through direct communication, in personal dialogue.

Dialogue should be:

affectionate, that is, based on the Mistress's disinterested love for the person of the young woman in formation;

respectful of the personal reality of each one;

understanding, able to take the point of view of the “you” in order to grasp the motives of her actions;

liberating, building on the person's positive qualities to point out the way to growth;

guiding, sensing the processes of life and moments of crisis, so as to lead the young woman to true self-acceptance.

Duration

55. In a context of personal formation aimed at the fundamental option, and in the light of the Instruction Renovationis Causam1027, it is thought fitting to allow greater flexibility in the length of the stages of the formation period. This will make it possible:

- to respond particularly to each person's own needs, respecting the dynamic of growth and maturing, which is not the same for all, and the work of Grace, which has no set duration;

- to give the young woman the opportunity to prepare for perpetual profession—the goal of the formation cycle—with greater inner maturity and a more conscious acceptance of the commitment she is making, without feeling forced by the rigidity of a fixed deadline.

D) Stages of formation

Postulancy

56. The Postulancy, as immediate preparation for the Novitiate, is an introductory period to Religious Life in which, in direct contact with our Communities and the Works of the Congregation, the candidate gains a clearer view of the life she wishes to undertake, and the Institute verifies the authenticity of the Postulant's vocational orientation, tests her degree of religious knowledge and fosters her gradual adjustment from secular life to the life proper to the Novitiate1028.

The chief task of this period is therefore to establish a right balance in the educational program, so that it is suited:

- to foster the candidate's human and affective maturing;

- to offer her the doctrinal elements needed to deepen her Christian life;

- to put her in contact with the Apostolic Work of the Congregation;

- to prepare her for the free and responsible choice of religious life.

The Postulancy, considered thus in relation to the Novitiate, will help the Postulant's human and Christian development, creating in her the conditions that enable her, by a responsible choice, to answer God's call and begin the Novitiate, aware of the breaks that religious life involves “with regard to persons and things”1029.

Novitiate

57. The Novitiate, with which religious life begins, is a period of probation whose aim is:

- “to make known to the novice the essential demands of religious life and the practice of the evangelical counsels which she will one day profess”1030;

- to foster the experience of encounter with God in prayer, in community life and in formative apostolic activity1031;

- to test realistically her aptitude for our way of life1032, preparing her in freedom and responsibility for the profession of religious vows, aware of the charismatic mission of the Institute, from which her whole inner life as a consecrated person and her apostolic activity must flow1033.

Novitiate: the backbone of formation

58. The Novitiate thus appears as an irreplaceable element1034 of the formation cycle, forming the backbone of the process of entry into religious life.

Indeed:

a) The society we live in does not give Christian values the absolute importance it gave them in other times, and young women who aspire to religious life, influenced by prevailing relativism, generally show a state of insecurity “which could undermine the values of religious life and of faith itself”1035. The Novitiate must therefore give Novices the opportunity for a living experience of the mystery of God's Fatherhood and, in an atmosphere of intimate and trusting supernatural serenity, root people in God and in the Institute. The family spirit, the soul of our charism, carefully cultivated in the Novitiate, fosters this experience, since it gives the setting the warm sense of home which, by satisfying the Novice's deep psychological needs, helps her achieve the fundamental synthesis of her life in Christ, as daughter of the Father and sister of all people, enabling her to work serenely toward the unity of her personality as a Daughter of Saint Anne.

b) Achieving “this unity presupposes a right understanding of the essence of the spiritual life and of the means that lead to closer union with God, expressed now in the solitude of intimate contact with the Lord, now in generous dedication to apostolic activity”1036. To this end novitiate life “will be permeated with inner life and silence and with attentive care for others”1037, so as to accustom the Novice to a deep attitude of contemplation and service, in imitation of Mary, who kept all things in her heart1038 and hastened to wherever her presence was needed1039.

c) The Novitiate is also a valuable element in the process of resocialization involved in entering religious life. Its character of separation and suitable seclusion1040, which involves sacrifice and effort, greatly fosters a sense of solidarity and belonging to the group, as well as the acquisition of the values and patterns of behavior proper to our Family. However, this separation, essential especially at first, must gradually become a balanced presence of the Novices among the Professed and a contact with the ecclesial community and the social environment, with a view to their progressive entry into apostolic life.

In the apostolic Communities.

specific preparation and apostolic training.

d) The Novitiate also includes formative apostolic periods spent outside the House of formation, “to the extent that, in the judgment of the Mistress and with the consent of the Major Superior, such periods seem useful for formation;... during these periods the Novices remain under the direction of the Mistress”1041.

Juniorate

59. This is a period between first profession and perpetual vows, whose aim is:

- to deepen the commitment of consecration, continuing the formation of the Novitiate in all its aspects;

- to lead the young professed to the degree of spiritual maturity needed so that, when pronouncing perpetual vows, the decision is made with full awareness and freedom, and inspired by enthusiasm and joy for the gift received1042;

- to give the juniors scientific and professional training, according to their aptitudes and the apostolic purpose of the Congregation.

60. The Juniorate, seen not only as a house of formation but rather as an overall period of preparation for Perpetual Profession and the apostolate, corresponds to the nature of religious vocation, which involves consecration to God and mission for the good of others, within the Church.

With a view, then, to achieving these aims, on which the future of the Congregation largely depends, “religious shall not be assigned to apostolic works immediately after the novitiate, but their religious and apostolic, doctrinal and technical formation, including the obtaining of appropriate degrees, shall be suitably continued in houses established for that purpose”1043.

This implies organizing the time of the Juniorate into periods of preparation and study in the Juniorate house and periods of apostolic training, which must meet the needs of each junior.

The Juniorate house should offer its own suitable setting that fosters unity and continuity of formation and be located in significant centers of social and cultural life; it should enable the juniors to attend courses of religious, academic and professional formation in order to obtain the specific qualification.

Apostolic training

61. Once they have acquired the necessary specific preparation, the Juniors will be sent to the various works of the Congregation. During this period, however, they will return to the Juniorate for a specially organized annual meeting, long enough to allow continuity and deepening of their formation1044.

While stressing the fundamental importance for a religious's formation of the period properly set aside for it (Postulancy, Novitiate and Juniorate), we cannot overlook the evident importance also of the first years of her integration into the community of professed Sisters. This integration, since it involves a change of setting and way of life, requires of the Junior a great capacity to adapt to new situations that may often disconcert her.

This requires particular attention on the part of the Community that receives her and especially of the Superior.

We cannot forget that Juniors, precisely because they are young, are very susceptible to the impressions and influences, especially negative ones, of their first community experiences; impressions and influences that will weigh heavily on their later conduct, for good or ill. Hence the duty and responsibility of these communities to help them overcome the difficulties of the first encounters through welcome and fraternal understanding, which must in no way be maternalism or systematic opposition, but a kindly interpretation of possible mistakes and a search for the truth and authenticity of their behavior through persuasive dialogue.

The community, then, must offer the young sisters the witness of an authentic community life, in which each shows herself ready to live the evangelical counsels to their ultimate consequences; in this way each sister, according to her specific mission, will help awaken in all an ever-growing enthusiasm for their common vocation.

Outline of the governing structure of the Institute

I. The Congregation of the Daughters of Saint Anne is a hierarchical, centralised religious society of pontifical right. In it supreme governing power, in the extraordinary line, resides in the General Chapter. In the ordinary line, Government is divided into three distinct and successively subordinate levels:

1st level (central Government): represented and exercised over the whole Institute by the Superior General, assisted by a group of Councillors, by a Secretary General and by a Bursar General.

2nd level (Provincial Government): represented and exercised in each Province by the respective Provincial Superior, assisted likewise by a group of Councilors, a Provincial Secretary and a Provincial Bursar.

3rd level (local government): exercised within each House by the respective Superior, who is likewise assisted by her own co-workers.

II. The General Chapter, the supreme extraordinary organ of Government, consists of an Assembly formed by the members by right (determined by the Constitutions) and by the Sisters delegated by all the Provinces according to the norms laid down in the Constitutions. This Assembly forms a collegial moral Person in which the supreme legislative and elective power of the Institute resides.

The General Chapter therefore:

- establishes the Constitutions;

- decides, in accordance with the Constitutions, on the most important matters concerning the life of the Institute and on any new orientations of a general character, always, however, according to the spirit of the Institute and the directives of the Church;

- reviews and, if necessary, amends the decisions of previous General Chapters.

III. Central Government, the supreme ordinary organ of government, is represented by the Superior General, assisted by her Council in the ways and forms laid down by the Constitutions.

The Superior General is the direct continuer of the work of the Mother Foundress and therefore represents the principle of the Congregation's unity. The Holy See and the Constitutions confer on her supreme and immediate power over every Province, House and Sister, by virtue of the Vow of obedience each one pronounces into her hands or into the hands of her Delegate.

Her task is:

a) to safeguard and strengthen the spiritual unity of the Congregation, guiding and carrying out the dynamic purpose of our religious Family so as to respect the purity of its particular charism, while listening attentively and docilely to the directives of the Church and to the “signs” that indicate the needs and demands of the times.

To this end she keeps in touch, by all the means at her disposal, with the Daughters working in the various parts of the world, and in particular, through direct and continuous relations, with each of the Provincial Superiors.

As often as possible she sends Circular Letters of a formative and informative nature to the individual Houses. At least once during her term of office she personally visits all the Houses of the Congregation.

b) To maintain devoted and filial relations with the Apostolic Holy See and to see that its directives are observed in the individual Provinces and Houses, as well as, within the limits allowed by the particular character of our Institute, the directives of the respective Ordinaries;

c) To promote and nourish the apostolic effectiveness of the Works and the zeal of the Sisters, both on the occasion of her Visits and by sending her Councilors to the various sectors of activity, according to the specific competence of each.

The General Council consists of the group of General Councilors, appointed according to the Constitutions, who together with the Superior General form the Central Government.

As far as possible, each Councilor should represent within the Council, with suitable qualifications, one of the apostolic and charitable sectors of the various Works.

Namely:

- the school and education sector

- the hospital sector

- the social-assistance sector

- knowledge of the general problems of the Spanish-speaking Provinces

- knowledge of the general problems of the Portuguese-speaking Provinces

This criterion makes it advisable that the General Council, which must also include the Vicar General, consist of six Councilors.

The General Councilors are the direct collaborators of the Superior General in the government of the Institute. This collaboration takes on juridical force when, in the cases and forms provided for by the Constitutions, they are called to give their opinion with a deliberative or consultative vote.

Outside these cases, their chief task consists in the assistance which, under the authority and according to the directives of the Superior General, they are to give to the Works of the Congregation, each within her own specific field, through suggestions, visits and every other suitable form of intervention and support. These relations between the Center and the Houses, while helping to preserve and strengthen unity among all parts of the Congregation, serve to keep the Superior General and her whole Council informed about the organizational efficiency and apostolic value of each Work, so that at the level of government it is possible, by coordinating all the relevant elements in relation to the overall activity of the Congregation and always in agreement with the Provincial Superiors concerned, to take the most suitable decisions for the good of each and all of the Works and Communities.

IV. Government at the provincial level is presided over and exercised by the Provincial Superior, assisted by her Council.

The Provincial Superior is, in her Province, a Major Superior with her own ordinary power in all that concerns the life and development of the Province, according to the Constitutions and in full and sincere communion with the Superior General, to whom she must look as the indispensable principle and center of the spiritual unity of the Congregation.

Within her Province, the Provincial Superior:

a) promotes with all her strength the spiritual progress of the Sisters, in keeping with the Institute's own spirituality but with due respect for individual freedom;

b) takes a direct and responsible interest in ensuring that the Works to which the Communities of her Province are devoted are genuine centers of evangelical charity and apostolic outreach. To this end she frequently visits the Houses entrusted to her care;

c) sees to the maintenance of a fraternal spirit between House and House, as well as between her own and the other Provinces of the Institute;

d) works to ensure that each House, while respecting its own spirituality and characteristic features, responds effectively to the needs of the local Church.

The Provincial Council functions within its Province in a way analogous to the General Council.

V. Government at the local level is presided over by the local Superior, whose chief task is to animate the faith life of the Community in fraternal charity and apostolic activity, and to safeguard common life and regular observance in the way best suited to the good of souls and the effectiveness of the works.

Her task is therefore essentially spiritual, and even in all that concerns the running of the Works and the administration of goods she must never lose sight of the particular purpose of every activity and of the very existence of the Community, which is common sanctification in the spirit of the Church and of the Institute.

The guidelines of her government are set by the Constitutions and the Directory, as well as by the general and particular directives given from time to time by the Major Superiors.

The various types of Local Council, according to the specific character of each Community, are determined by the Directory.

notes.docbase-en-fn740: Fili d'Oro, p. 239: “Daughter Superior, be cheerful: the Lord loves you; try to respond by keeping the Rules and having them kept by your sisters, those whom God has entrusted to you...”
notes.docbase-en-fn591: Fili d'Oro, p. 249: “Daughter, I hope to find you cheerful and wholly transformed into Saint Anne; her true disciple: her speech, her countenance, her gaze.”
notes.docbase-en-fn711: Gal 6:1-4: “Brothers, if anyone is caught in some fault, correct him in a spirit of gentleness; and look to yourself, for you too may be tempted... for if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. Rather, let each one examine his own conduct and he will be convinced that he must judge himself more humbly, refraining from boasting in comparison […]”
notes.docbase-en-fn815: John 15:5: “...whoever abides in me and I in him bears much fruit...”, and Mother Rosa: “Without prayer we are barren trees and can give nothing good, and our fruits (if we bear any) will always be unripe” (Fili d'Oro, p. 113).
notes.docbase-en-fn699: P.O. 8: “Each one... is therefore united with his confreres by the bond of charity, prayer and unconditional cooperation, thus showing that unity by which Christ willed his own to be one.”
